summary: C: The avatar keeps re-litigating the decision to recruit a bandit at all, out loud, in front of Jost, apparently unaware or unbothered that he's standing right there for it. Jost, unbothered in turn, just waits for them to finish. B: The avatar admits the re-litigating isn't really about Jost -- it's the habit, they do it to every call whether it worked out or not. Jost points out that's exhausting to watch and probably worse to live inside, and offers the one thing his own approach has going for it: once a thing's decided, sleeping through the rest of the argument is free. A: The avatar admits they've never once managed to just let a decision be decided; Jost admits his own version of that isn't peace, it's refusing to spend anything on a question after the fact because spending on it before never worked either. Neither talks the other into changing. The avatar starts running fewer post-mortems out loud where Jost has to hear them; Jost starts actually staying awake for the ones that are about him.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich). Scorpion's failure mode ('carries it long after it stopped being useful') set directly against Ram's virtue (decisive, doesn't look back) -- two opposite relationships to a decision once it's made. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar reviews Ricberta's levy reports and flags the handwriting as suspiciously clean for a dictated report; Ricberta deflects, badly, in a way that would fool someone with less reason to notice competence being hidden. B: The avatar doesn't push it in front of the levy, which Ricberta clocks as deliberate -- an administrator who argues everything in the open chose not to, this once. She starts wondering what else the avatar's decided not to argue about, out loud, for someone's sake. A: The avatar admits they know exactly why she's hiding it -- rank protects nothing once someone above you decides your competence is a liability, and they've watched it happen to smarter people than either of them. Ricberta, who's spent years managing the secret alone, gets the first offer of institutional cover from someone with the rank to actually make it stick: the avatar will vouch for her literacy being an asset, not a flag, whenever she decides to stop hiding it. She doesn't take the offer. She does, for the first time, believe someone meant it.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun). Direct tie: Ricberta's own note ('secretly literate... literacy is a deputy tiebreak') is exactly the kind of hidden-competence-as-liability the avatar's own institutional position lets them actually shield, unlike the peers who could only ever gossip about it. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar keeps re-auditing Emmerich's own audits, on principle, which Emmerich reads -- correctly -- as a vote of no confidence in his single most anxious competency. B: The avatar admits the re-auditing isn't about Emmerich specifically, they do it to everyone's work, everywhere, always -- which Emmerich finds almost worse, since it means the scrutiny he's been dreading personally was never personal at all, just weather. A: The avatar concedes the point and tries something new: they ask Emmerich to flag his own uncertainties up front instead of waiting to be caught, which turns the audit from a test into a conversation. Emmerich, who has spent his whole tenure terrified of exactly this kind of scrutiny, discovers being asked is different from being checked on -- and starts actually volunteering the numbers he's least sure of, since for once nobody's using them against him.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Emmerich=Lion from Jost/Emmerich). Scorpion's habit of relentless scrutiny turned from adversarial to collaborative, directly defusing Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') by changing what being watched means. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar wants Waldrada's defection formally on record, decided, filed -- loyal to diadem, full stop, so the roster stops flagging her as a question mark. Waldrada tells them the filing would be a lie; she's still deciding, and has been for years. B: The avatar, who never lets a settled question stay settled, finds this almost funny -- they'd assumed endless deliberation was Waldrada's flaw and their own habit of reopening closed questions was the opposite problem. Waldrada points out it isn't the opposite at all: neither of them can leave a question alone, they just picked different questions to never finish. A: The avatar admits they reopen decided things because closing them feels like giving up the chance to get it right; Waldrada admits she's never closed hers because closing it feels like giving up the chance it was ever going to matter which way she chose. Neither one finishes deciding anything by the end. They do start comparing notes on how to live functionally inside a question that never resolves, since apparently that's both their whole method now.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda). Scorpion's failure mode ('carries it long after it stopped being useful') recognized as the same shape as Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') from the opposite direction -- reopening vs never closing. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar keeps re-pushing an already-overruled requisition for more winter-dole grain. Maren, who runs the dole line, has heard every version of this argument already, from people with more rank and less follow-through. B: Maren notices the avatar doesn't stop arguing once the requisition is denied a second time -- goes over the ledgers alone, at night, still building a case nobody asked to hear again. She starts leaving the real capacity numbers where they will find them. A: The avatar admits the arguing was never strategy -- walking away from a wrong call feels like the actual failure, rank or no rank. Maren, who has watched people put on a Warden's mask specifically so they can keep making that same call without it costing them anything, tells them plainly: don't go numb to it, get useful instead -- and hands over the dole line's real numbers, unfiltered. S (romance): the avatar stops arguing to be right and starts arguing with Maren's numbers instead of past them; Maren, who pours herself out for a whole line of strangers every winter, finds the one person she doesn't have to ration the truth for.
notes: Avatar=Scorpion is new, off the avatar's own note ('level 1 administrator... voiced and argumentative'), read as someone who keeps re-raising a decision everyone else has let rank settle, which is the Scorpion's virtue ('carries the grudge that keeps everyone honest') read institutionally rather than personally. Maren=Crab is new, off her own note ('winter-dole healer' -- loyalty to the people in her line over the crown's actual allotment, the Crab's own failure mode read as triage under scarcity) -- a deliberate second Crab, distinct from Ricberta's (military/secrecy) by being medical/scarcity-driven instead. Assembly-route avatar option per the original skeleton note; the avatar's sign is treated as fixed across both avatar chains in this pass, the same convention already used for an established unit's sign (Kest, Rinsa), not reassigned per pairing.

summary: C: The avatar keeps proposing improvements to Brandt's gate rotation, in detail, repeatedly, each version slightly different; Brandt holds the gate the same way regardless and lets the proposals pile up unread. B: The avatar, unused to being simply ignored rather than argued with, corners him about it. Brandt's answer is plain: the gate's held every time so far, and a new rotation on paper doesn't hold anything until it's tested, so he's not going to trade a working method for an untested one just because it's newer. A: The avatar admits the proposals were never really about the gate -- it's the habit, improving things whether or not they're broken, because standing still on a decided question feels like negligence. Brandt tells them plainly that's not negligence, that's most of what holding actually is -- deciding once, correctly, and then not needing to keep re-deciding it every day. The avatar doesn't stop proposing improvements everywhere else. They do let Brandt's gate alone, and start noticing which of their own decisions might already be as solid as his.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig). Scorpion's failure mode ('carries it long after it stopped being useful') meets Bull's virtue ('holds ground nobody else could') as a direct model of a decision that doesn't need reopening. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar wants their own decisions recorded in the archive alongside everyone else's, formally, the way Edda records units' histories; Edda points out that's not really what the archive's for -- it's for the roster, not the administration. B: The avatar, who never lets a boundary like that sit unquestioned, pushes on why the distinction matters. Edda tells them plainly: a record of the decision-maker starts shaping the decisions to look good in the record, and she's not going to be party to that, even accidentally. A: The avatar admits, after arguing it six different ways, that she's right, and that the impulse to be recorded was itself a version of the thing she's protecting against -- wanting the archive to already have an opinion about them before the actual history's finished happening. Edda offers a compromise instead: she'll record the decisions, not the decider, no names attached until much later, when there's enough distance to write it honestly. The avatar, for once, stops arguing and takes the compromise exactly as given.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Edda=Maiden from Waldrada/Edda). Scorpion's compulsion to keep re-raising a settled question meets Maiden's own discipline (accuracy over flattery) directly -- one of the only chains where the avatar loses an argument cleanly and accepts it. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar asks Dietmar, bluntly, whether the gate-holding deed is a real strategic priority or a favor to an old soldier's ego. Dietmar, who has spent the obsolescence arc waiting for exactly this question and dreading it, doesn't dodge -- he just doesn't answer it either. B: The avatar keeps pushing, the way they push everything, and Dietmar finally admits he doesn't know the honest answer himself, which unsettles him more than the accusation would have. The avatar, who has never once let an unresolved question sit, recognizes something familiar in a man who's been avoiding his own for longer than the avatar's been alive. A: Dietmar admits the deed matters to him whether or not it's the correct use of the diadem's resources, and that not knowing which is the actual failure of the obsolescence, not the fading itself. The avatar, whose whole method is arguing until something resolves, doesn't resolve it for him -- just tells him some questions are worth keeping open on purpose, since a man who stops asking whether he still matters is worse off than one who keeps asking and doesn't like the answer yet. Dietmar takes the deed anyway. He stops needing it to be the right call to be worth doing.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Scorpion's virtue ('carries the grudge that keeps everyone honest') applied to an institutional question rather than a personal one, directly confronting Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully'). Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar keeps trying to formally reassign Torvald to somewhere with an actual current mission, citing efficiency; Torvald keeps declining, politely, without explanation, every time it comes up. B: The avatar, unable to let an unresolved assignment sit, pushes for the reasoning. Torvald finally gives it: his post isn't a mission he was assigned, it's the last thing connecting him to men who don't exist anymore, and reassigning him would sever that on paper the way the plague already severed it in fact. A: The avatar, whose whole method is arguing a thing until it resolves, doesn't argue with this one. They admit efficiency was never actually the point of the proposal, it was the same compulsion that makes them re-litigate everything -- an unclosed assignment nagged at them the way an unclosed question always does. Torvald tells them some things aren't inefficiency, they're just what's left, and not everything left needs resolving into a cleaner shape. The avatar leaves the assignment as it is. It's one of the only unresolved things on record they've ever let stay that way on purpose.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Torvald=Crab from Dietmar/Torvald). Scorpion's compulsion to resolve everything meets the one situation where resolving it would be the actual harm -- Crab's loyalty read as something that shouldn't be optimized away. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar wants Rinsa's account of the descent formally, for the record, the way they want everything -- structured, arguable, citable. Rinsa gives them the same answer she gives everyone: the descent isn't the kind of thing that survives being made into an argument. B: The avatar, who has never once accepted 'some things don't reduce to a case' as a real answer, keeps pressing, and Rinsa finally asks them plainly what they're actually trying to settle. The avatar admits it's the Venerated question -- they need it to be decidable, because the whole administration they're running depends on eventually deciding it. A: Rinsa tells them the descent doesn't decide anything either, it just goes down and comes back, same as it always has, for anyone -- the deciding was never hers to do, only the witnessing. The avatar, whose entire method is deciding things, has to sit with a source who refuses to resolve into a verdict on command. It doesn't change the avatar's strategy. It does change how they ask the next question, and the one after that -- less like a case to close, more like a person they're actually listening to.
notes: Avatar=Scorpion reused from Avatar/Maren. Rinsa's own already-stated sign, the Vessel, reused verbatim. Direct tie to the endgame: Rinsa's own note calls her 'the only unit who has BEEN down there' regarding whether the Venerated is dead, and the avatar's own note ('voiced and argumentative') makes them exactly the kind of person who'd try to litigate that fact instead of just receiving it. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Kest cases the avatar's own field desk out of habit before she's decided whether to join at all. The avatar catches her at it and, instead of reporting it, asks what she'd have taken. B: The avatar keeps re-litigating a call from chapters back -- a defection let stand, a resource not seized -- out loud, to no one in particular. Kest recognizes the arguing-with-someone-not-there rhythm immediately and says nothing, which is its own kind of recognition. A: Pressed, the avatar admits the second-guessing isn't doubt about the decision, it's refusing to let a bad outcome go unexamined just because it's over. Kest, still withholding her own reason for the same habit, offers only that she used to think the arguing meant something was wrong with her. The avatar's answer -- that it just means the argument mattered enough to keep -- is the first thing anyone's said about it that isn't trying to fix her. S (romance): the avatar's grudge against its own decisions and Kest's grudge against her own survival stop being separate arguments -- two people who never let a thing go finally aim it at the same target instead of at themselves.
notes: Kest's sign (the Twins) is her own already-stated sign, reused verbatim, not reassigned -- same treatment as in the Rinsa/Kest chain. Avatar=Scorpion reused from the Avatar/Maren chain above (see that chain's note for the grounding). Diadem-route avatar option per the original skeleton note.

summary: C: Ricberta doesn't trust the ford bandit the diadem just recruited, says so to his face, and expects him to either sulk or lie about it. Jost does neither -- agrees with her, cheerfully, and goes back to sleep. B: Jost keeps proving decisive exactly when the levy needs it and useless every other moment, which Ricberta, who's spent her whole career being the useful one nobody notices, finds harder to forgive than if he were simply bad at the job. A: Ricberta admits what actually bothers her -- Jost gets to be exactly what he is, unpolished and unbothered, while she's spent years managing a secret just to keep her post. Jost's answer surprises her: he tells her the sleeping is the only unpolished thing about him left, the rest -- the timing, the read on a fight -- he built on purpose, the same as she built her reading in secret; it just doesn't look like work from the outside. Ricberta stops mistaking his ease for laziness, and starts running her levy's ambush drills past him first.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun). Both diadem-route, ch_d02/ch_d03 -- a freshly-recruited ex-bandit and the levy sergeant who has every institutional reason to distrust him. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's requisition ledgers keep coming up short after Jost's unit passes through. Jost's defense: he only takes what the count had already lost, not what's tracked -- which Emmerich hears as a personal insult to his ledger's accuracy. B: Jost, constitutionally unable to sit through Emmerich's line-by-line reconciliation meetings, starts falling asleep in them -- except Emmerich notices he only sleeps through the parts that don't matter, and stays sharp the instant a real number comes up. A: Emmerich admits the tidy showcase reports are half theater -- the Baron needs the diadem line to look competent more than he needs it accurate, and Emmerich is the one stuck producing both at once, terrified of the day the gap shows. Jost's answer isn't reassurance, it's a second set of eyes: he starts double-checking Emmerich's counts himself, badly, at a bandit's honest pace, so someone besides Emmerich is watching the real number. S (romance): Jost stops treating the ledger as a thing to raid and starts treating it as Emmerich's, specifically; Emmerich stops needing the Baron's audience once Jost's sloppy, loyal recount is the one he actually trusts.
notes: Jost=Ram is new, off his own note ('ford bandit; lucky sleeper' -- decisive the instant an ambush needs him, constitutionally unable to sit still for anything that isn't one -- the Ram's virtue/failure pair exactly). Emmerich=Lion is new, off his own note ('requisitions clerk; Baron showcase' -- a subordinate whose composure depends on being visibly valued by a superior; the Lion's failure mode, 'cannot take a demotion gracefully,' would hit him hardest of anyone on the roster). Both diadem-route (ch_d02/ch_d03), consistent with the original skeleton note.

summary: C: Waldrada, still weighing a decision from years back, asks Jost how he ever manages to just act without running the whole calculation first. Jost's answer -- he doesn't run any calculation, ever -- sounds to her like either the freest thing she's heard or the most reckless. B: Jost admits the not-calculating isn't really freedom, it's that the one time he did calculate carefully, it went wrong anyway, so he stopped trusting the math. Waldrada, whose whole method is trusting the math forever without ever finishing it, recognizes a version of her own problem running in the opposite direction -- both of them let one bad outcome decide how they'd handle every decision after. A: Waldrada admits she's never actually let the defection be finished because finishing it would mean living with whichever answer she picked, good or bad, same as Jost avoiding the calculation because he can't stand living with a wrong one. Jost tells her plainly that a decided thing, even a wrong one, is still lighter to carry than an undecided one forever -- he knows, because he's spent years proving it by carrying nothing at all. Neither fixes the other's method. Waldrada starts letting some smaller questions actually close. Jost starts running the calculation on the ones that are worth it.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda). Ram's virtue (decisive, doesn't look back) and Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') both traced back to the same root: a single bad outcome that taught each of them the wrong lesson about deciding at all. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Tancred, fresh into the Pardoner line and taking absolution seriously, corners Jost about whether he regrets the banditry. Jost's honest answer -- not really, it kept him fed -- is not the answer Tancred was hoping to practice forgiving. B: Jost, watching Tancred grind through the Pardoner line's unglamorous requirements with real effort, admits he doesn't understand doing hard, boring work for a payoff that's mostly spiritual. Tancred doesn't try to convert him; he just keeps climbing, visibly, in front of Jost, which needles Jost more than a sermon would have. A: Jost admits the sleeping was never really laziness -- it's that trying and failing at something that mattered once cost him more than he could afford to keep paying, so he stopped trying at anything he couldn't walk away from clean. Tancred, who measures people by what they build rather than what they've survived, tells him the climbing doesn't have to be for something -- his own is mostly just proof he's still capable of it. Jost doesn't take up the climb. He does start showing up to watch, which is its own kind of practice.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm). Both diadem-route village-adjacent recruits (ch_d03), opposite relationships to their own pasts -- Jost's own note ('lucky sleeper') read as someone who stopped trying at anything he couldn't walk away from clean, set against Tancred's own note ('Pardoner line') as someone who took up trying, deliberately, as its own discipline. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Jost, newly diadem, meets Brandt on a joint assembly-diadem detail and clocks him immediately as the kind of soldier who'd have made his old ford ambushes a lot harder. Brandt, unbothered by being sized up by a reformed bandit, agrees, and asks if that's a compliment or a complaint. B: Jost admits it's a compliment, mostly -- he respects competence he can't get around, more than he respects competence he can. Brandt, who's used to being underestimated rather than flattered, doesn't quite know what to do with being professionally admired by a man who used to rob people for a living. A: Jost explains the respect plainly: Brandt's the kind of obstacle that would have made him actually plan instead of just getting lucky and sleeping through the rest, and Jost's spent his whole life avoiding exactly that kind of pressure. Brandt tells him that's not nothing -- most people never find out what they'd be if the easy way stopped working, and Jost's at least honest enough to know he never found out either. It's not quite a friendship. It's two men being plainly useful to each other's self-assessment, which for both of them is rarer than friendship.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Jost, half-asleep as usual, asks Solveig what it's like to already know how a flight's going to go before you take off. Solveig, prickly about the prophecy, tells him it isn't like that at all -- then admits she's never actually been asked the honest version of that question before. B: Solveig watches Jost sleep through the parts of a briefing that don't matter and snap awake the instant something does, and asks how he decides which is which without ever seeming to decide anything. Jost's answer -- he doesn't decide, it just arrives -- sounds uncomfortably close to her own family's account of the prophecy, except his always seems to serve him and hers never asks what she wants. A: Jost admits the sleeping isn't really about instinct, it's that deciding things in advance never worked out for him, so he stopped bothering and let the moment do the deciding instead -- which is either wisdom or the same trap her family's in, and he's honestly not sure which. Solveig, who has spent her whole life being handed an answer she didn't get to earn, tells him that not-deciding is a kind of freedom she's never once had, prophecy or no prophecy -- and asks him, seriously this time, to teach her how he does it, on purpose, instead of by accident.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Solveig=Vessel from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Ram's virtue read as decisiveness-without-premeditation, set directly against Vessel's failure mode ('belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody') -- inherited certainty vs earned spontaneity. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Anselm, working through a crisis of total ambivalence, asks Jost how he ever decides anything without agonizing over it first. Jost's honest answer -- he doesn't decide, mostly, he just reacts when it counts and ignores the rest -- sounds to Anselm less like an answer and more like a diagnosis of his own condition from a totally different angle. B: Anselm admits the caveats that used to feel like honesty now just feel like never landing anywhere; Jost, unbothered by landing or not landing, tells him that's the difference between them -- Anselm's still trying to get the whole picture right before acting, and Jost gave up on the whole picture a long time ago, which is either freedom or failure and he's genuinely not sure which either. A: Jost admits the not-deciding cost him things he still doesn't examine closely; Anselm, whose whole practice right now is examining things closely and finding no bottom, tells him that not examining it might be the more honest response to a question with no bottom, not a lesser one. Neither converts the other. Jost starts asking one more question before reacting, some of the time; Anselm starts letting a caveat go unspoken, some of the time. Neither one calls it progress. Both notice it anyway.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Anselm=Fishes from Tancred/Anselm). Ram's virtue (decisive, doesn't look back) offered as an unintentional answer to Fishes' failure mode ('understands the enemy too well to fight them') -- not resolving the doubt, just modeling a different relationship to acting inside it. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Kheldar, cataloguing which recruits might be useful contacts later, marks Jost down as a dead end -- a reformed bandit with nothing left to leverage, no debts, no angles. Jost, hearing about the assessment secondhand, is oddly pleased to be considered useless to a professional manipulator. B: Kheldar, curious despite the assessment, asks how a man builds up literally nothing worth holding over him. Jost's answer: he never kept anything long enough to owe for it, not money, not loyalty, not grudges -- travel light, nothing to lose, nothing anyone can take. A: Kheldar admits, almost enviously, that his own whole trade depends on everyone having something to lose, and he's never met anyone who genuinely doesn't. Jost tells him plainly it isn't a trick, it cost him the chance to actually want anything too, same as it cost him the ability to be leveraged -- the emptiness cuts both ways. Kheldar, who has spent his career being the one thing nobody can pin down, recognizes the same nothing looking back at him from a totally different angle, and for once doesn't try to find the angle in it.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest). Ram's own decisiveness read as an absence of anything to lose, directly undermining Scorpion's whole professional method (leverage via grudges and debts) -- two versions of having nothing held over you, one costly, one useful. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Dietmar, reviewing the diadem's new recruits, is visibly unimpressed that a reformed bandit made the roster; Jost, unbothered, sleeps through the inspection instead of defending himself. B: Dietmar, expecting either an argument or an apology, gets neither, and finds himself oddly rattled by a man who simply doesn't perform for his approval. He asks Jost outright why he doesn't bother trying to impress him. Jost's answer: trying to impress people who've already decided about you never once changed the outcome, so why spend the energy. A: Dietmar admits that's the exact opposite of his own entire method -- he's spent the obsolescence arc trying to impress people into remembering he still matters, and it's cost him more than Jost's indifference ever could. Jost tells him plainly some audiences were never going to change their minds regardless, and the trick isn't winning them, it's noticing which ones are actually worth the energy. Dietmar doesn't stop trying to matter. He does start being pickier about who he's trying to matter to.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Ram's virtue (decisive, doesn't look back, doesn't perform) as an implicit rebuke of Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') -- indifference to an audience as an alternative to needing one. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: They meet over dispatch schedules -- Sigrun keeps delivering orders faster than Ricberta's levies can act on them, and Ricberta's clipped complaints about 'impossible timing' are the whole conversation, on the surface a logistics gripe. B: Sigrun notices what nobody else on the levy roster does -- Ricberta reads the requisition slips before anyone reads them to her, a beat too fast for someone who's supposed to need them read aloud. She doesn't say it in front of the others, which is its own kind of answer. A: Ricberta admits it outright, expecting the usual calculus (a literate sergeant is a sergeant someone above her will want moved, watched, or replaced). Sigrun's response isn't reassurance, it's redirection -- she starts routing dispatches so Ricberta's own reading gets used instead of hidden, folding the secret into the job instead of asking Ricberta to keep choosing between them. S (romance): what holds is exactly what the signs promised and neither one flinched from -- Sigrun says the true thing at the worst moment, and the worst moment turns out to be the only time Ricberta would have believed her. Loyalty that used to end at 'the people already inside the wall' widens by exactly one.
notes: Signs assigned per the signs tab's own methodology (argued from behaviour, not a keyword): Ricberta=Crab off her own note ('secretly literate... literacy is a deputy tiebreak' -- guards a secret to protect her position and the people under her, the Crab's own failure mode -- loyalty to people over the cause -- is the exact shape of hiding competence to keep her sergeant's post rather than risk promotion scrutiny). Sigrun=Archer off hers ('courier rider' -- ranges out, returns with news, the Archer's failure mode 'says the true thing at the worst moment' is the literal action that breaks the support open in the B->A transition).

summary: C: Tancred, deep in his order's discipline about honesty, asks Ricberta -- not unkindly, just directly -- whether hiding her literacy from her superiors counts as a kind of lie she should be confessing to someone. Ricberta tells him flatly it's none of his order's business. B: Tancred admits the question was clumsy, but the concern under it wasn't -- he's watched enough people in the diadem get quietly punished for competence to understand the hiding, he just wondered if it cost her something to keep confessing it to no one. Ricberta, expecting a lecture and getting an actual question instead, admits it does cost something, just not the thing his order would call sin. A: Ricberta tells him plainly what it costs: not guilt, just the specific loneliness of a secret with nobody keeping it alongside her, only for her. Tancred, whose whole practice is unglamorous, witnessed work, offers the one thing he actually has to give -- witnessing, no confession, no absolution required, just someone who knows and doesn't report it. Ricberta doesn't confess anything new. She does let one more person carry the knowing, which turns out to be most of what she needed.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun, Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm). Crab's failure mode (a secret carried entirely alone) met by Goat's virtue (unglamorous, witnessed work) reframed as simple witnessing rather than confession -- Tancred's class instinct corrected by Ricberta's actual need. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Maren needs Ricberta's levy roster locked in for dole allotments; Ricberta, protective of exactly how much information about her men gets shared upward, gives her a partial list and calls it complete. Torvald tells her plainly it's not nothing -- the standing is the news, some days; a post held is its own kind of dispatch, delivered to no one, and still worth riding past to confirm. summary: C: Sigrun, professionally curious about anyone who travels somewhere and comes back with something, asks Rinsa what the descent is actually like to ride, courier to courier. A: Sigrun, whose whole worth is in what she brings back and how fast, admits she's never once thought about what it costs to be the medium and not the message -- to matter only as the route, never the news. Rinsa tells her that's exactly right, and exactly fine; being the road is its own kind of necessary, and Sigrun of all people, whose job is also being a road for other people's urgent things, should already know that isn't nothing. summary: C: Tancred, deep in the Pardoner line's early discipline, tells Waldrada plainly that defection is exactly the kind of thing his order exists to forgive. summary: C: Maren, running the dole line during a cold snap, needs Waldrada's flight roster locked in fast; Waldrada, still weighing whether the diadem's logistics are even trustworthy enough to commit her route to, is late with the answer and costs the line an hour. Waldrada admits it's the same question it always is: which side actually deserves the commitment. A: Maren tells her plainly that the dole line doesn't have the luxury of that question -- she decided a long time ago who she's loyal to and it was never the crown or the assembly, it was the people in front of her, and Waldrada could try deciding the same way instead of weighing institutions against each other forever. summary: C: Anselm, doubting everything these days, asks Waldrada how she's managed to keep re-litigating one decision for years without it dissolving into total uncertainty about everything else too. Waldrada tells him it hasn't dissolved -- if anything it's the only thing she's certain is still unresolved, which is its own kind of stability. Waldrada asks what the original question even was, and Anselm realizes, saying it out loud for the first time in a while, that he's lost track; the doubt outlived the question that started it. A: Waldrada tells him plainly that's the actual danger in what they're both doing, not the doubting itself -- hers has stayed contained because she's never let it spread past the one decision, and his has swallowed everything because he let it. Anselm, hearing the difference named clearly for the first time, starts trying to locate which specific questions are actually open and which ones he's just been carrying out of habit. Waldrada tells him that's easy for a man who's never actually committed to a side; she gave something up permanently, and he's never given up anything he couldn't smuggle back out again. A: Kheldar concedes the point -- his whole trade is built on never being pinned to one position, and he's never had to find out what it costs to actually choose and live inside the choice. Waldrada admits what it costs is exactly what he'd expect: years of wondering, with no way to test the alternative. Neither one envies the other's method by the end. They do agree, for once, that the other one's found a genuinely different way to survive the same uncertain world, and neither is obviously the wrong way.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest). Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') set against a man built entirely around never being pinned to one position -- committed permanence vs perpetual adjustability, neither one resolved as superior. summary: C: Dietmar, revolution-generation to his core, has opinions about defectors; Waldrada, freshly defected from the assembly, has heard every one of them already and isn't interested in his verdict. Waldrada, who's spent the same stretch of time unable to say outright which side she serves, recognizes someone else performing a loyalty he isn't sure he still feels. A: Waldrada tells him plainly that deliberation isn't the same as disloyalty -- she took years weighing it and the assembly earned every year of doubt. Dietmar, who has never once let himself weigh it, admits her question is the one he's been outrunning since the gate-holding deed started feeling more like a museum piece than a duty. Neither talks the other out of anything; they just stop being each other's evidence for a verdict neither one wanted to reach alone.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald above). Both diadem-route (ch_d01/ch_d02) -- a defector and the veteran who's built his whole identity on never having been one. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Waldrada, still weighing whether her defection was right years after making it, asks Rinsa -- half joking -- if the oracle takes questions about decisions already made. B: Waldrada admits that's exactly her problem -- she can't tell anymore whether she's still deciding or just refusing to let a decided thing be decided. Rinsa, who spends her whole professional life watching people descend with exactly one real question and come back changed by finally asking it, tells her the weighing itself might be the tell: people with an actual open question don't usually take years circling it. A: Waldrada admits, plainly, for the first time, that the defection was decided a long time ago and the circling since has been about something else entirely -- not knowing what to do with a choice that can't be undone. Rinsa tells her that's not indecision, that's grief for a version of herself who might have chosen differently, and grief doesn't resolve by more deliberation, only by being let alone to run its course. Waldrada doesn't stop thinking about it. She stops treating the thinking as a decision still in progress.

Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') correctly diagnosed by Rinsa's professional expertise (someone who watches people actually resolve questions for a living) as something other than deliberation entirely. summary: C: Tancred asks Maren for a blessing over the dole line, formally, Pardoner-style; Maren tells him blessings don't move grain and she doesn't have time for the ones that don't. Neither changes what they do. Both change what they think they're doing it for.

Solveig, hearing her situation correctly named as outside his order's whole framework for the first time, feels less alone in it rather than more, just from being accurately placed instead of misfiled as guilt. Gunnar doesn't understand the question; the work was always the point, not what it led to. Gunnar tells him plainly that climbing and improving aren't the same thing, and it's worth being honest with himself about which one he's actually doing. Gunnar, who has never needed to be seen moving to know he'd gotten better, offers the only correction he has: keep climbing if the climbing's real, just check the math against the work itself, not the rank, the way an old huntsman checks a shot against where it actually lands, not where it was aimed. Tancred keeps climbing. He starts keeping his own private ledger of the work itself, separate from the rank, to make sure the two don't quietly drift apart.

summary: C: Edda wants to record Tancred's progress through the Pardoner line for the archive, the way she records everyone's; Tancred, still early and unsure any of it's worth recording yet, asks her to wait until he's actually built something worth writing down. Tancred admits he's been treating the record as a reward for arriving somewhere, not an account of the getting there. B: Tancred admits the caveats are the only part of Anselm's theology he's started to trust -- a monk who insists on his own uncertainty is at least not lying to him, unlike the men Tancred grew up under. Anselm, for the first time, says something without immediately qualifying it. Tancred, who measures people by what they've built, refuses to measure Anselm by what he's stopped being able to do. Tancred's climb gets a companion who won't let him mistake the climbing for the point; Anselm's dissolved certainties get one fixed thing he doesn't have to argue himself out of.

Goat's own failure mode (measures people by output) is the exact friction the A-support resolves by Tancred explicitly refusing to apply it.

summary: C: Tancred, still new enough to the Pardoner line to take it seriously, tries to extract a confession out of Kheldar for the manifest fraud everyone quietly knows about. Kheldar finds the attempt almost sweet and declines to be absolved of a sin he doesn't consider one. Kheldar, unused to being pursued without an angle, starts actually answering the questions instead of deflecting them, if only out of professional curiosity about a man who wants nothing from him. Tancred doesn't ask to see it; he tells Kheldar that's closer to penance than anything Tancred's own line teaches, since nobody assigned it to him and nobody's grading it. Kheldar doesn't confess to anything. He does, for the first time, let someone watch him not lie about not confessing.

Direct moral-code friction: Tancred's own note ('village recruit; Pardoner line') is explicitly a forgiveness/penance class line, set against Kheldar's own note ('manifest discrepancy thread') -- a penitent and an unrepentant profiteer, deliberately not resolved into either converting the other. summary: C: Dietmar, watching Tancred grind through the Pardoner line's early, unglamorous requirements, tells him plainly that nobody remembers the grinding, only the finished thing -- advice meant kindly, from a man whose own finished thing is starting to be forgotten anyway. B: Tancred asks, carefully, whether that's actually true, since Dietmar himself seems to be finding out it isn't. Dietmar admits the finished thing fades faster than the grinding ever did in his own memory -- the revolution's a name now, the years of actual work before it are the part he still remembers clearly, alone, since nobody else was there for that part either. A: Dietmar tells him, revising his own advice: remember the grinding on purpose, keep it for yourself, because it may be the only part that's still yours once the finished thing becomes everyone else's story to tell. Tancred, who measures people by what they build, realizes Dietmar's obsolescence isn't really about the revolution fading, it's about losing ownership of his own history to the legend of it. He starts asking Dietmar for the ungrinded version, the real one, specifically so someone besides Dietmar has it too.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Goat's virtue (measured by what's built, the unglamorous middle) offered as the corrective to Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') -- ownership of one's own unglamorous history as a hedge against becoming someone else's legend. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Tancred, deep in his order's discipline, tells Kest plainly that a life of theft is exactly the kind of thing that needs building away from, one honest job at a time. Kest, mid-argument with herself as always, surprises him by agreeing with half of it out loud before catching herself. B: Tancred asks which half she agreed with. Kest admits it's not really about theft, it's the 'building away from' part -- she doesn't know how to build toward anything, only away from things, and has never once let herself imagine what an honest life would actually look like day to day instead of just what it wouldn't be. A: Tancred, who measures people by what they build rather than what they've fled, offers her something concrete instead of a sermon: come watch what his own building actually looks like, day to day, unglamorous, nothing like the redemption story she's picturing. Kest does, expecting to be unmoved, and finds the boredom of it more convincing than any argument would have been -- an honest life turns out to be smaller and less dramatic than the thing she's been arguing herself out of. She doesn't take it up. She stops arguing herself out of it being possible.
notes: Tancred=Goat reused from Tancred/Anselm. Kest's sign (the Twins) is her own already-stated sign, reused verbatim. Goat's virtue (unglamorous work, measured by what's built) offered as a concrete counter-example to Twins' failure mode ('won't commit while a better argument exists') -- showing rather than arguing. summary: C: Brandt's shield arm takes a hit that should have ended his rotation for the week; Maren, running the dole line short-handed, patches him fast and rough and tells him to sit down before she makes it an order. Maren, who's spent her whole practice deciding which people get her real attention instead of her rationed attention, makes her decision plain: she starts teaching him the forms that turn a shield-sergeant into someone who can actually take the hits he's been absorbing on will alone. The Great Shield he earns after isn't hers to take credit for. It's the first time either of them built something instead of just enduring it.

summary: C: Solveig's courier runs keep clipping the dole line's schedule, forcing Maren to reorganize around whenever the prophecy family needs the sky. Maren complains once, sharply, about being reorganized around someone else's inheritance. Maren gets her schedule. Solveig gets the strange, small satisfaction of being the exception to her own pattern, on purpose, for someone who just asked plainly instead of deferring.

B: Anselm admits he can't finish a blessing without a caveat lately, doctrine gone loose in his hands, and watching Maren work without any of his doubt looks like a mercy he's lost the knack for. Maren corrects him: it's not certainty, it's that she decided a long time ago which people she's loyal to, and the dole line always wins the tiebreak. Anselm, whose whole practice has become sitting in the doubt rather than hiding it, offers her the one thing his theology's actually good for: permission to not have it worked out yet and keep working anyway. It's the first time anyone's told her the mask doesn't have to be a wound.
